questiontext.text:
Claim: for every integer \(n\) with \({@lo@} \le n \le {@hi@}\), \[2^{n/10} > \left(\dfrac{n}{10}\right)^2.\]

Enter the set of all \(n\) in this range for which the claim is false. Type a set in curly brackets, for example {5, 6}; type {} if there are none. You may use a calculator.

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A claim about every integer in a finite range is proved, or disproved, by checking every value in the range. Here is the check, with values to 3 decimal places.

[[foreach row="tablerows"]] [[/foreach]]
\(n\)\(2^{n/10}\)\(\left(\dfrac{n}{10}\right)^2\)Claim true?
{@row[1]@}{@row[2]@}{@row[3]@}{@row[4]@}

The claim is false for every \(n\) in {@ta1@}. At \(n = {@eqn@}\) the two sides are equal (both are {@2^(eqn/10)@}), and a claim that one side is greater than the other fails when they are equal. A check of only some values in the range could have missed this.

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the first example under Potential mistakes (2^(n/10) and (n/10)^2 for 10 ≤ n ≤ 20), p. 20, in Section 5 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

node.description: Diagnostic: equality counted as greater than

truefeedback.text: [[if test="emptyp(diag1)"]]The claim says greater than. Is there an \(n\) in the range where the two sides are exactly equal? At such an \(n\) the left-hand side is not greater than the right-hand side, so the claim is false there.[[else]]Every \(n\) you have entered is right, but one is missing. The claim says greater than, so it is also false at any \(n\) where the two sides are exactly equal. Is there such an \(n\) in the range?[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text: Check every \(n\) from {@lo@} to {@hi@}: work out \(2^{n/10}\) and \(\left(\dfrac{n}{10}\right)^2\) and see whether the first is greater. For example, at \(n = {@ntrue@}\), \(2^{n/10} \approx {@lhstrue@}\) and \(\left(\dfrac{n}{10}\right)^2 = {@rhstrue@}\).
